utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. It was hoped that we were going to be able to sit on Monday, but I understand, Mr. Robinson, that that's impossible because of pre-arranged Defence conferences; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't -- actually, we do have one conference between 2.00 and 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That was when we were going to try and sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So that obviously negates that because the conference, I understand, was the witness who was to immediately follow on -- from that conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Then we'll simply have to press on. Thank you. Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness. Is it true -- true that you proposed changes and amendments to the agreements on DMZ and the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not quite correct. The changes I suggested were essentially changes in the establishment of the weapons collection points. We felt that the idea and principle on which these centres were based did not enable us to control these weapons the way we wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind just to confirm. We already explained that. To whom did you suggest it -- this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that you proposed this to the Serbian side and that the Serbian side did not respond.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't entirely remember this affirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're seeking a redaction of lines 10 and 11, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of reply did you get from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D2483. There's no need for it to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a document that was forwarded to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can look at the rest of the pages, but I have no further questions relating to this document. I just want it to be admitted into evidence along with your reply that you received no response.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The document's been identified and there's no doubt to its authenticity so we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1122, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We mentioned some disruptions in supplies provided for the city. Yesterday, I showed you a UN document saying that the Muslim side was opening fire at a cargo plane. The Defence submits that very often the Muslim side obstructed the provision of supplies for the citizens of Sarajevo in order to blemish the Serbian side, to create a crisis, and to disrupt relations. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my level, I found myself operating on the ground, which means that I relied on facts. I was trying, with the UN forces on the ground, to be as objective and impartial as I possibly could. I don't know what the general policy was above me. What I do know is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, and I'm really interested in hearing all this provided we had time. My question was: Did you know that the Muslim side obstructed the provision of supplies for the citizens of Sarajevo in order to tarnish the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty of the UN forces was to ensure free circulation of the supply convoys. Any obstacle obstructing these free movements were obstacles which we tried to do away with, whether these obstacles be physical or psychological.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any obstacles on the side of the Muslims? Did they disrupt the provision of supplies for their own citizens? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which would enable me to answer a positive yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're now going to show you a series of UN documents that show this, and to that end can we have 1D3366 in e-court, please. This is a report on the observation of the cease-fire agreement in March. If we recall, this was an agreement brokered by President Carter. Can we go now to page 4. To your estimate, how many convoys used to pass through, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the passage rate, or the proportion of convoys due to arrive and those that actually reached their destination, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We already have the answer. This UN document says that Bihac received 29 per cent, Sarajevo 71 per cent, Srebrenica 93, Zepa 80 per cent, and the last place, 80-something per cent. Do you agree that the Serbs did not hinder much the passage of these convoys?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These figures undoubtedly -- I'm not familiar with this document. This document relates to a particular period of time. I don't see where the assessment date of these convoys is mentioned. This was during a fairly calm period, as far as Sarajevo was concerned. This figure seems to me to be a reasonable figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 2 of this document. Take a look, please, concerning the restoration of utilities. "[In English] Continuing efforts for the restoration of utilities yielded limited results. In Sarajevo there was little progress, but neither was there much erosion; gas, electricity and water are all available at relatively abundant levels." [Interpretation] Do you agree, Mr. Witness, that these were the benefits of the Carter cease-fire that was still in force more or less, and as one can see, the Serbian side did not present any obstacles and that life in the city was tolerable.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should put the question to the residents of Sarajevo whether this was bearable or not. I'm not sure that they felt that at the time. But I would like to specify this: As far as the restoration of utilities, electricity, and so on, let me remind you that a number of UNPROFOR soldiers were injured. They were shot at when they were trying to conduct repairs. Not during the period --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Witness. Mr. Witness. Does this document indicate that -- or still in March there was cease-fire brokered by President Carter and that the supply of water, electricity and gas was tolerable? Can you tell me just that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period, that is correct. There was a relative lull at the time, and life was probably easier at this time than at other times, as I mentioned in my consolidated statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted? And at the end of the document, there is a chart showing which side was in violation, and there were no innocents in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has affirmed part of the document, and it's an official UN document. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on. Can we now have 1D3367. The Carter truce is still in force, but let's see how the situation deteriorated. This is a telegram sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan, dated the 7th of April, 1995. Can we now look at page 2. Let's take a look at paragraph C: "[In English] The airport routes were open, tram services were running and the utilities were beginning to be repaired and maintained. All progress came to a halt due to the referral of the Bosnian side to attend the Central Joint Commissions, designed to negotiate, amongst other things, the status of Sarajevo. The flagrant disregard of the COHA by the BiH when they launched two military offensives in the Travnik and Stolice areas also contributed considerably to the worsening situation in Sarajevo. Additionally, the killing of two Serbian children by sniper fire within Sector Sarajevo influenced and hardened BSA attitude."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm waiting for the interpretation. Now, is this consistent with what you and your people knew about the situation in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the attacks in Travnik and elsewhere are concerned, I don't remember, since this was not within the Sarajevo area of responsibility. As far as the obstructions on the Bosnian side because they wished to be part of the commissions, admittedly they were -- did not agree with the fact that we should continue with the negotiation as had initially been planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Again, the document appears to be affirmed in general terms, because -- and it is again an official document. We can admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3365. The date is the 17th of April. It's a reply by Mr. Annan to Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the second sentence in paragraph 2. "[In English] We would be grateful if you would provide a comprehensive assessment of the actual supply situation in the safe areas both for UNPROFOR and UNHCR. According to your daily sitreps, UNPROFOR continues to have access by land convoys, although we note the absence of fuel deliveries in recent days. Preliminary information obtained from UNHCR likewise seems to indicate that humanitarian supplies in principle do not appear to be running low. We hear they are currently meeting 75 per cent of their targets." [Interpretation] Does this correspond to the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the figure mentioned here seems right. That would apply to the end of April. After that, it's a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we'll see later why it was different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's probably not necessary, Dr. Karadzic, because you've read the important part into the transcript and the witness has affirmed it, so it's -- the important part's in evidence anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3369.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know that the obstacles for convoys imposed by the Serbian part were always based on specific grounds that the Serbian side made clear and announced in advance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll leave this document for later. Can we now have 65 ter 17721. 65 ter 17721.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a daily report addressed to the Security Council, dated 9th of June. Number 1 says: "[In English] The UNHCR, UNPF, UNPROFOR delegation to Pale held more than six hours of discussions yesterday with Drs. Karadzic and Koljevic. They successfully negotiated an agreement to start delivery of humanitarian aid by land routes to Sarajevo as soon as possible. The text of the joint statement issued to the media is as follows: "'A crucial agreement has just been reached between the Bosnian Serb authorities and UNHCR to allow the resumption of humanitarian aid deliveries by land to the people of Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Et cetera. Do you recall that this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I wasn't in the loop of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Akashi is writing to Mr. Annan. You were not there but somebody from UNPROFOR must have been there because we have here the participants listed, i.e., UNHCR, UNPF, and UNPROFOR. The two top men of Republika Srpska were working for six hours towards reaching an agreement which was ultimately reached. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report states that there were UNHCR representatives and UNPF and UNPROFOR representatives present. Not only was I not aware of this meeting, but nobody reported to me what had been said at that meeting. The only thing I did know is that an agreement had been signed, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official UN document, and I'd like it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, again, Dr. Karadzic, the document's been identified. The part you wanted the witness to agree to, that there had been a negotiated agreement, is now in evidence, but the witness couldn't go further than that. It seems to me that the matter you wanted is again in evidence in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That brings me into a situation that I have to read longer passages than I would have liked, but I accept what you said, and I would just like to make note that this was an official telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't actually require that. What it requires is, Dr. Karadzic, that if you're going to read something in, you simply stick to what you regard as the critical points, and if the witness adopts them, so be it, but you don't have to read the whole of the document. I'm simply trying to cut down the number of exhibits that are not necessary to admit in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, this whole document is significant. This was a telegram exchange between two key figures, Annan and Akashi. I would like you to reconsider admitting the whole document, because we might find ourselves in a situation in the future that we would have to tender it into evidence after all. Can we look at page 2, which shows that it also arrived in Zepa, and Zepa was also important. Page 2, please. It says here, paragraph 4: "[In English] A UNPF convoy of one truck and one APC arrived at Zepa at 1935 hours last night carrying rations and fresh food. The Ukrainians now have about 25 days supply. The convoys supplying the sectors in Croatia," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Therefore, the whole document is significant, and it shows that these shortages were not exactly as they were being portrayed. It says here: "[In English] Convoy supply in the sector in Croatia are now running at a normal rate again. Sarajevo has less than two weeks of fresh food."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, you asked for the document to be admitted having dealt with page 1. If you want to ask the witness about matters concerned on page 2, of course you're free to do so. It's better to do that before you ask for the document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree and do you know that on the 9th of June -- or, rather, the 8th of June, a convoy reached Zepa and that this document confirms that the Ukrainians had enough supply for the next 20 days?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the supply of Zepa is concerned, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender it into evidence now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, and if you'd done that in the first place before asking to admit it, then the answer would have been yes then. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're right, but I'm endeavouring to save time. Can we now have 1D3369. That's another Akashi's telegram sent to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see how this convoy of the 8th of June passed through and reached Zepa. That was an UNHCR convoy. Look at this document where it says exchange of fire, Sarajevo, and then paragraph 4: "[In English] UNHCR convoy to Zepa was stopped by the BSA at Rogatica. Three small boxes of ammunition were reportedly found in the convoy. We have no more details at this time. The convoy to Srebrenica reached its destination with 72 metric tonnes of humanitarian aid." [Interpretation] My question, Witness, from earlier was -- which I didn't actually put to you clearly enough, is this: This smaller number of convoys that had difficulties, was it always stopped with some reason that the BSA army reported to UNPROFOR, saying the reason is such and such? Would you agree with that? Did you receive any kind of explanation from the BSA for convoys that were not let through?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNHCR convoys, with regard to them I only had information when they reached their destination. I was only told that it had arrived, without further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this convoy passed through even though ammunition was found? Not a significant number, three small boxes, but the convoy did arrive, nevertheless, at its destination in Zepa as the document states.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did confirm that that convoy had arrived, and if it had arrived, that meant that it had gone through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we will see what the United Nations felt was the reason for the difficulties in supplying the town of Sarajevo. Can we now look at 1D3374, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of course, you are familiar with the name of Philip Corwin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him by name, but I didn't know him personally. But I am aware of his name, yes. I'm familiar with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please ask you to look at the following at the first paragraph: "[In English] At the very last minute, the Bosnian side, this afternoon, rejected a proposal to restore utilities to Sarajevo. The Serbian side had agreed to the necessary technical arrangements arranged by Mr. John Fawcett from the Office of the Special Coordinator for Sarajevo. But the Bosnian side insisted on UNPROFOR control of Bacevo ..." [Interpretation] And it goes on to say: "[In English] ... as relates to several gas supply points ..." [Interpretation] And then it goes on to say in the second: "[In English] In the meantime, the utilities should be restored but the Bosnian side refuses, and at the end they even try to link restoration of utilities to food convoys." [Interpretation] Paragraph 3. "[In English] It appeared that the Bosnian side did not want the utilities restored. There are several reasons. "By keeping their own people in need, they hope to gain world sympathy. The press is on their side and one can expect CNN (Clearly Not Neutral)." The CNN abbreviation is "Clearly Not Neutral," and so on. [Interpretation] Did you know that the Muslim side wanted to increase the suffering of its population in order to gain some benefit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to answer because I was not part of the drafting of this document. I did not participate in the meetings. I was not among the addressees of this message. So I can't tell you or confirm that this is a correct document at all. I don't know anything at all about it. I have no information that would make it possible for me to say to you that this is a fair reflection of reality, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 4, please: "[In English] As for the Serbs, they had requested the meeting, and were clearly in favour of restoring the utilities. Our guess is that the 100.000 citizens of Serbian Sarajevo are suffering badly, and are quite annoyed with their blood(y) brothers in Pale." [Interpretation] Blood brothers as in relatives, I think, not bloody brothers. This is an intervention for the translation. This is quite a major thing, sir. You and other witnesses also talked about the difficulties in supplying the citizens of Sarajevo. The position of the Defence is that these difficulties were caused by the Muslims, because it was to their advantage to have a bad image of Sarajevo in the media, and it was not to the advantage of the Serbs. Would you agree that the media image of the suffering in Sarajevo was to the detriment of the Serbian side and an advantage for the Muslim side in Sarajevo? This is something that you mentioned in your statement as well.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I said that I did not pay attention to what the media would say, and my reasoning was not based on information from the media. As for this document, I repeat that I'm seeing it for the first time, and the position as stated by Mr. Corwin to be sent to the UN authorities is his own personal opinion. I'm not here to cast judgement on what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that this is not a personal letter but it's an official dispatch? Can we scroll down a little bit this page so we can see the letterhead. Is this an official dispatch by Akashi?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope this is an authentic document. If it is now displayed on the screen, I guess it is, but I never had an opportunity to read it. It was not addressed to me, and there was not even a copy meant to be sent to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this? It is a United Nations document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It is a United Nations document, but -- and I don't suppose that the provenance or authenticity is going to be in doubt, but this witness hasn't confirmed anything on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but I mean I would be -- he's been examined about various portions of it and asked to respond to it. At least in some respects it will have to clarify that, for example, the document identifies what Bacevo was, which was not made clear. Also the accused's intervention to blood and bloody was inaccurate. It's obvious that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, it's an attempt at humour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, and at making a point about the perception of the Pale leadership. So I note that in connection with the admissibility issues, but I take the Court's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's -- taking the Court's point is -- is a Delphic way of saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I made it clear I don't object to the admission, but I'm not trying to battle the Court in its ongoing attempts to control document admissibility pursuant to guidelines it deems appropriate, but from our point of view, no, there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No. Well, strictly speaking, the witness didn't confirm it. On the other hand, it's an authentic document. The issues which it relates to are important issues, and it seems to me on balance as a matter of fairness we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the parties, it's explained in parentheses what Bacevo is. It's the main source of water that was located on Serbian territory. Thank you. Can we now have 1D3373, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned on a number of occasions the difficulties regarding UNPROFOR's freedom of movement. Were these difficulties caused only by the Serbs or were they caused also by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to tell you to what extent it was one or the other party's cause, but there were difficulties arising from the Serb and also from the Muslim, caused by both. You know, 16 years after the events I can't have an exact recollection, but I can tell you that both Serbs and Muslims would put obstacles to our free movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this report by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan of the 16th of June, and the second sentence in the first paragraph states: "[In English] UNPROFOR's freedom of movement has been restricted by the proliferation of the BiH check-points in the city and its ability to assess the situation further diminished by the lack of the OPs within the area." [Interpretation] A bit lower. "[In English] Clearly the BH actions are intended to break the current efforts of the UNPF/UNPROFOR to stabilise the situation and return to the status quo ante. Thus, whether or not the BiH are in a position to break the siege of Sarajevo could be irrelevant to their calculations as -- if their actions prompt the usual overreaction by the BSA on the city of Sarajevo, international sympathy for their cause will become further reinforced, calls for stronger action against the Serbs louder, and criticism of the UNPF/UNPROFOR's inaction more strident. They could well be gambling that images of Sarajevo being pounded by Serb mortars could influence domestic opinion in the US, pressurising President Clinton to reverse his decision on the unilateral lifting of the arms embargo." [Interpretation] Witness, sir, do you recall that with the offensive initiated by the Muslim side on the 15th of June there was an obstruction in the co-operation of the Muslim side and the forces and elements of the United Nations in the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can confirm, and this document is a general document of which I was not aware today, the only thing I can confirm is that indeed movement within the city of Sarajevo for UNPROFOR units was limited by Muslim actions within the city. This I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. It did occur to me that when such large portions of a document are read in, I'm not sure there's any efficiency advantage to not admitting it. I think that probably in the end it's easier for the parties and the Court to access the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit the -- admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It may not be particularly pertinent with this witness at this time, Dr. Karadzic, but sometimes in order to save time it might be worth finding out whether or not the witness can read the document to themselves quickly and that would save time, but the point that Mr. Tieger makes is very accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Can we now have 1D3370.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also a telegram by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan of the 16th of June. Can we now look at page 2. This is the supply situation as it relates to the city, and it's a meeting between representatives of the United Nations, UNPROFOR number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- on page 1, and it states here that: "[In English] I undertook to consider possible alternatives in order to accommodate the wishes of the Bosnian government but did not rule out any option consistent with the relevant Security Council Resolutions. Presumably Muratovic's opposition to UNPROFOR convoys passing through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is based on two considerations: The government's wish to maintain the isolation of Belgrade as well as Pale; and its wish to see the perpetuation of the logistic crisis in the enclaves, prompting us to consider more extreme resupply measures." [Interpretation] Could you tell the Trial Chamber who Mr. Muratovic is, whom you perhaps had meetings with?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet him. As far as I know, he was the minister in charge of European relations. Well, of co-operating with the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A minister in the Muslim government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. He was a minister of the Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that now we might have to move to private session just briefly, and then we're going to tender this document. So can we move to private session just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the second page of the document that we were looking at earlier, and this can be broadcast now. Do you see that in this paragraph Mr. Muratovic, in a telegram of the United Nations, sent by Akashi to Annan, and Akashi probably received it in turn from the UN in Sarajevo, states that Muratovic is not interested in supplies via Yugoslavia for political reasons in order to isolate Belgrade as Pale. Is that something that conforms with your knowledge about manipulations of the humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot pass judgement as to what was in the mind of Mr. Muratovic. The only thing I can confirm I confirmed earlier on. He seemed to be somewhat disinterested with regard to Srebrenica, and he found it difficult to ensure free movement within the city of Sarajevo. As for the rest, I can't express any judgement at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3376 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, again, this is a dispatch from Phillip Corwin to Mr. Akashi, in Zagreb, experiences with the Serbian side about the same questions. And then we have the first paragraph: "[In English] I had a long talk with Professor Koljevic this afternoon in Pale. He said that President Karadzic was very eager to meet with Carl Bildt. The Serbs considered that the situation was deteriorating, especially with regard to humanitarian aid, and they wanted to meet urgently." [Interpretation] This is the 6th of July as we can see. Can we scroll down this page, please. And now can we look at the following page. "[In English] Koljevic seemed genuinely eager to establish contact with Bildt. He repeated several times that he was concerned about the deterioration -- deteriorating humanitarian situation." [Interpretation] And at the bottom, the last sentence, the last two sentences of paragraph 7 in the English, I will read them: "[In English] Clearly he and Karadzic are not happy with having lost power to the military, but they are also not happy about the course that the military might take." [Interpretation] Do you know -- does this sound familiar to you? Do you know that there was this meeting with Professor Koljevic and do you confirm that Professor Koljevic was the number 2 man in Republika Srpska, he was the vice-president of the Republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at all of the meeting so I cannot confirm what was said during that meeting. The only thing I know is that Dr. Koljevic was indeed the number 2. That is what I had been told, but I met him only once at a meeting, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see here that the recommendation to Mr. Akashi here is that Bildt should come to Pale, and if not to Pale, then to Zvornik? Do you remember that there was the position for the Serbian side in Bosnia to be isolated in order to negotiate with Belgrade rather than with Pale?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, you're showing me a document, and you are casting a judgement on it. I cannot confirm it at all, because this was not within my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, you spoke about a number of things that you didn't see and that were not in your jurisdiction, so I wonder that you don't have any information about what was being attempted to do with the Serbs, namely to isolate them. Are you able to confirm that the situation was worsening in July, the humanitarian situation was worsening, and that what Professor Koljevic said to Mr. Corwin was correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting. I can therefore not confirm what was said. The fact that the situation deteriorated is true in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the witness simply can't confirm anything about this document. He's agreed with the point that you've made, but the document itself is something he's not able to express an opinion on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please, in your amalgamated statement, as well as on some other occasions, you -- excuse me. I have to go back to the previous document. Mr. Witness, you claimed that the Serbian side had the strategy of terrorising the citizens of Sarajevo, whereas it was the Serbian side who proposed meetings that would alleviate the plight of the citizens and improvement -- improve the humanitarian situation. Did you know that the Serbian side had a positive attitude towards the process of restoring the utilities and that the Serbian side had a positive attitude towards the passage of convoys and that that was in contravention of the conclusion that it was the Serbian side who was bent on terrorising the citizens of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to move into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: (redacted) [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber] improve the humanitarian situation. You can see that 29 per cent of humanitarian aid passed through the territory not under our control, whereas between 80 and 90 per cent of convoys pass through our territory. So if only you looked at the UN documents, you could have found out exactly what Mladic's position towards Sarajevo was instead of second guessing. On the other hand, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm afraid you're not asking questions. You're attempting to give evidence. You're arguing with the witness. None of this is of any assistance at all. The witness has given a specific answer, and pass on, please, to a question -- a genuine question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With all due respect, Your Excellencies, I'm asking the witness, and I am pointing to a discrepancy, a contradictory position; that is to say, that he was trying to guess what the Serbian intentions were. I am asking you whether the command was making this up or did they receive this information from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was only -- I think the Court has made the point, but I was going to note that in the face of the Court's observations that the accused was making commentary and arguing and the admonition to ask questions, the accused then continued the argument but this time with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You pre-empted me, Mr. Tieger. Dr. Karadzic, there's no point in you arguing with the witness. There's even little point in you arguing with the Court, and none at all in arguing with me. Now please go on to a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, then it's better for me to argue with the Prosecutor's office, because Mr. Tieger's intention is obviously to worsen the situation. I think we can revert to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we'll revert to open session, but comments like that are simply unhelpful and time wasting. You're acting as counsel. Please behave like counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you, Witness, that your position was that the Serbian side in the total exclusion zone had calibres that were in violation of the provisions of the zone, whereas the Muslim side had artillery pieces of calibre below 12.7 millimetres? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information was based on reports coming from my units and the visible actions we were able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, look at page 47 of your amalgamated statement, somewhere in the middle of the page where you say. "[In English] The weapons used by the Bosnian side were weapons lower than 12.7 millimetres." [Interpretation] And you say that that was the information you had received from your subordinates; is that correct? Do you still maintain this position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that the reports indicated that other reports did not perhaps indicate that a higher calibre was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court 1D3375. This is also addressed to the UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb on the 18th of June, 1995. Can we now have page 4 of this document. Item B -- no, no. It should be page 5, not page 4. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at these highlighted portions where there is mention of the violations of the total exclusion zone. Look at the assessment down there: "[In English] The situation is expected to stay uncertain and tense. It's still unclear whether BH offensive will continue or not. Current condition on WF's activity allows to conclude that BH did not get the expected results." [Interpretation] And downwards, fire incidents: "[In English] During the last 24 hours, most firing incidents were observed in Igman, Butmir, Sharpstone, Sedrenik, Osijek, Ilidza, Dobrinja, Mojmilo, Svabino Brdo, S of OP-1, airport, Nedzarici, and Log bus stop areas. Some explosions also reported today in Igman, Butmir ..." [Interpretation] And so on. Could you please look yourself at this portion which was encircled.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think that these explosions could be caused by ammunition of 12.7 millimetres and below, or are we talking about higher calibres?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document does not specify what kind of explosive device or calibre was used. These were observations made by the unit as regards the sounds they heard, but the calibre is not specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we do agree that there was no explosive ammunition below 12.7. If it is an explosive ammunition, it must be over 12.7 millimetres. No --

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the report in this instance does not specify what kind of calibre was used. When you talk about an explosion, these might be due to mortar explosions or infantry shells or shots fired.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have ERN page 297. That's four pages forward. That's not the right page. Within this same document, if I can have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this column marked with red pencil, and can you explain what this column signifies?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the -- the firing observed and coming from both sides. Firing incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is talking about explosions. One hundred and forty-four; correct? But what about the last column? What does this signify?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last but one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are weapons. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose weapons are these? Are these the pieces below 12.7, or are these explosions caused by artillery pieces of the calibre in excess of 12.7 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... weapons might have been used. I can't tell for the time being. It is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at it. Column number 1, warring factions. Second column, small arms. Third column, machine-guns; and the fourth column, HY --

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- does that stand for "heavy weapons"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... assessment conducted by the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are overlapping. I'm sorry, we're not making pauses. Therefore, could you please confirm that column number 1 is warring factions; number 2, small arms; number 3, machine-guns; and the fourth one, heavy weapons? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By definition, heavy weapons implies calibres over 12.7; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It is above 12.7. This was recorded as an explosion and was not checked. The units passed value judgement on the type of weapon used but did not check or did not see what kind of weapon was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the last column it says that 100 shells exploded in the Serbian territory, whereas 44 exploded in the Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back one page, please. Do you agree that this table indicates freedom of movement on the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I believe that this is a correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this table also shows that not a single bus had reached the Serbs but that between Sarajevo and Igman we can see the vehicles pass in the last three rows, which is 14 cars, 13 cars and 11 trucks, and the last one -- or, rather, a total of 27 cars and 25 trucks --

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- whereas on the Serbian side it was 0? Is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The witness has confirmed that he considers it to be a correct document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3378.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 3 of this document. I'm going to read it out loud. 18th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on paragraph 8, which is encircled and which says that the government offensive commenced on Tuesday [as interpreted] morning with heavy exchanges of mortar and artillery fire along the Hrasnica-Ilidza-Hadzici-Ilijas access. These places, were those places within the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are in the zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene. Can we seek a redaction at page 30, lines 20 through 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Witness, but it's important that the redactions are dealt with as they arise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that the Hrasnica-Hadzici-Ilidza line was in the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say that as the attack progressed it became evident that that was an attempt to break through the siege of Sarajevo -- "[In English] ... that the main thrusts of the attack was aimed at forging a passage through Hadzici in addition to the secondary objectives of cutting or interdicting the Bosnian Serb main supply routes into the city."

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems, doesn't it, Mr. Witness, that you were wrongly informed in the light of what you said on page 47 of your amalgamated statement: "[In English] The weapons used by the Bosnian side were weapons lower than 12.7 millimetres."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the accused please repeat the portion in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that out of the exclusion zone fire was opened at us using larger calibres?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the information wasn't perhaps quite correct, but as far as the attacks are concerned, it is clear that what was observed by the units was the following: The actions conducted by the Serbs were greater in number than the actions conducted by the Muslims, but the Muslims did also conduct actions and mortar fire and artillery fire was exchanged. The origin of the weapons had not been checked or seen by UNPROFOR units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell us, during that period that you are familiar with, which particular offensive was mounted by the Serbian side, and if so, can you provide evidence to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question today. I do not clearly remember all of this and cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have the next page of this document. Look at paragraph 9. "[In English] The launch of the attack coincided with the greatly enhanced security measures whereby a general alert was introduced and the existing curfew was extended to run from 9 p.m. to 6.00 a.m. daily. Check-points in and around Sarajevo were closed and UNPROFOR vehicles were denied access to the logistic supply route across Mount Igman." [Interpretation] In your statements, did you notice what was being done by the Muslim army both to us and to you? Did you highlight this fact in your statements, and did you notice that this offensive launched in June by the Muslim army had effect both on your supply routes and on your movement around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier in my testimony that we -- our movement was restricted in Sarajevo, which was the area where we operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have time for a few more questions, or do we need to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, we intend to break at 10.30. If you can ask a short question, take us up to then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's better if we take a break. I don't want to rush through the document, which is rather lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So you're confirming, Dr. Karadzic, you don't have short questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The document is a long one. The questions are going to be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We will take a break now for 30 minutes until 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I understand you have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We just wanted to alert the Chamber that with respect to the next witness, KDZ354, two proofing notes were prepared yesterday and they were not able to be transmitted to Dr. Karadzic until today, and he still hasn't looked at them because we've been -- from the minute he arrived, which was about 10 minutes before the session started, we've been working on this witness's exhibits and trying to cut them down. So we're not really in a position where he can cross-examine Witness KDZ354 today, and I wanted to let you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What's the extent or volume of these supplemental matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's about four pages, but it covers a fair amount -- we could provide them to you if you'd like to see them. It covers a fair amount of -- a few different incidents of this witness. It's something that we -- if it was overnight, I think we would be able to deal with it, but the fact that it's the same day, I think it's a little unreasonable to expect him to have 15 or 20 minutes to read it and incorporate it into his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Something you and I did every day, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe you, but I always asked for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I agree with the Court's observation. It also, you know, implicates the ongoing issue of the accused taking on every responsibility for himself by his own volition, but more importantly, this information is going to be led live. I don't think there's going to be difficulty incorporating that into the accused's understanding of the events and ability to deal with it at the time. It's discrete issues not related, as I understand it, to the bulk of the witness's evidence. I think it will be apparent to the Court at the time that we can proceed, and even in the event, which I don't think will occur, that the Court considers that cross-examination on those discrete issues needs some brief period of time for assimilation given the timing of the court, that's probably -- that can be deferred to the end of the cross-examination, which, based on the schedule, is probably going to occur at the very end of the day or the first thing tomorrow anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that seems likely, and, Mr. Robinson, let's for the moment make no hard and fast decisions but play it by ear. There is a -- I appreciate, it is a pressure, but there is, after all, another 30-minute adjournment coming up, and let's see if this can be done. In any event, we are hoping -- it's not been confirmed yet, to sit until 3.00 today. Yes. Have the witness back in, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as part of that, I'm hoping that the Trial Chamber will give me a little bit more time, because there are many documents and areas that we have not illuminated with this witness. I note that his statement is large, 100 pages, lots of interviews, lots of superficial or generalised assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, again, that will be something we'll consider on its merits once the time allotted has expired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Witness. Sorry for the short delay. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of a manoeuvre by the Muslim forces in the town of Sarajevo to position themselves very close to UN installations and to residential areas so that the civilians and the United Nations would serve as a shield for them and then they could fire from those positions at the Serbs in an attempt to get the Serbs to retaliate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether they wanted to use the civilians and UNPROFOR soldiers as shields, but what I know is that they indeed would put themselves as close as possible to UN forces, in particular close to the confrontation line. They wanted to involve and put themselves deliberately that way, embed themselves in that way to give the impression that there were in locations where such embedding could carry with itself serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if they were fired at when they were close to you or in civilian areas, would that create the impression of the town being terrorised?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether that was the consequence to be drawn from that, but I know that that -- when they would fire or have response fire to UN positions, the latter being dovetailed with the will of the Bosnians to be as close as possible to the UN positions. So they were also finding themselves in the midst of the population. There was a total mix of the UN forces, of the population, and the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call 65 ter 23033. I believe that this can be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the date and also the recipient and the person who is dispatching the message. Can we look at page 5, please. It's this assessment, the second paragraph. I'm going to read it in English. "[In English] ABH proceeds using of UN locations in the city as shield for deployment of the heavy weapon what provoke BSA retaliatory fire and jeopardise civilian -- civilians and UN troops. As confirmation mentioned we observed mortar fire originated from the areas of the TV building and PTT nearby the headquarters Sarajevo." [Interpretation] The rest everyone can read. Do you recall -- and here it is stated somewhere that they are very, very close. Do you remember this report? And does that reflect your knowledge as well as the position of the sender?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this report precisely, but I know the author. I can see the author's name here, and I think this reflects the situation as it was to be found on the ground on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D3384 once again but can it not be broadcast, please. 1DD3483 [as interpreted]. It's in English as well. Can we look at page 8 in the English. 1D3384. Page 8, please -- or, actually, seven from this one and 8 with the cover page where paragraph 63 is. One more. [In English] Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 63. I am going to read if from the second sentence on. "[In English] The big ambiguity as well as for Sarajevo was that Bosnian wanted very often to be the closest to the United -- UNPROFOR forces. I noticed that many times in Sarajevo, especially during a night when we received 3.000 missiles when the Bosnians were at 1.5 metre to the UN [sic] forces." [Interpretation] Do you stand by this position stated in that statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm this. This was in Debelo Brdo. There was a UN post there, and gradually it had been eroded by the Bosnian forces, and basically the UN forces and the Muslim forces were dovetailed, sort of interwoven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to 65 ter 23033, which we were looking at a little bit earlier. Can we look at the ERN page 030, last three digits, or page 9 of 14. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, just like in the previous document but now this is for the 28th of June, does this not show the table of freedom of movement, and that, as we can see, the Sarajevo to Igman route was crossed by a total of --

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the numbers of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this lower chart shows that the Serbian side did not receive anything, that nothing was let through to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. What had been observed by the UN units in charge of observing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page. That same table speaking about the machine-gun and heavy weapons and explosions, and the Serbian side used 92 to 74, but on the Serbian territory, more exploded in the Serbian territory, 295 compared to 91. So more shells exploded on the Serbian side. Do you agree that Muslims were able to fire at us in the exclusion zone using their weapons which were actually located outside the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at Annex C in this report, indeed there were explosions. As to the exact calibre and as to the origin of the fire, that probably was not specified in the various reports, but I do confirm this document saying that there were explosions in the Serbian zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The witness has confirmed the contents, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that we have to move to private session for this question. And can we have 1D3384 in the e-court once again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's establish that this is an UNMO report of the 12th of April, 1995, and it pertains to Zepa. It reads: "[In English] Officially, inside the demilitarised zone Zepa, no troops should exist. However, UNMOs have been reporting since the signature of the cease-fire agreement in 1993 that armed groups still remain inside the pocket. UNMOs confirmed in several occasions the presence of armed people, but regular troops, units, are not reported so far. The former local commander Colonel Avdo Palic is the man responsible for the control of the military situation and the troops. UNMOs confirm that the local B and H headquarter the existence of a Comcen with radio and Capsat equipment. It is estimated that the strength of the troops in pockets about five Coys." Did you know anything about this and were you in touch with this person?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, but it wasn't during this period at all, I received a phone call and talked to Colonel Palic, but this must have been in July, I believe, or as far as I remember. I remember the reports of the Ukrainian units very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second encircled paragraph speaks about a developed black market which the UNMOs of the United Nations find to be of concern. They are also talking about the local Mafia and the fact that certain incidents confirm that there was involvement on the part of the authorities but that it was yet unclear. Did you know about this, and were you able to obtain certain information from the military observers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this, all the more so that the UN observers were part of a different military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did meet them at joint briefing sessions; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we have to stay in private session for the next document, which is 1D3151. For your information, my point is that we were accused of imposing restrictions of food reaching Zepa. However, there was a food black market as well. Can we now go to page 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you recall that the strategic idea of Mr. Silajdzic was to have the Serbs enter Zepa and bloody their hands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we're still in open session, so we must go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you have an opportunity to see for yourself that the fact was that Mr. Silajdzic's idea was for the Serbian Army to enter Zepa and bloody their hands, even though he was in favour of the evacuation of population, but he was nevertheless keen to have the Serbian Army bloody their hands on his people.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. I'm not in the shoes of Mr. Silajdzic. (redacted) (redacted) I'm not quite sure what it is you want me to react to. Could you please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to go to private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning your last answer, Mr. Witness, is it true that United Nations, together with the Muslims who took Krupac illegally, entered negotiations with them and that the Muslims withdrew without sustaining any losses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations cannot say whether there were any casualties on the other side. What I do know is that military action was launched against Krupac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslims remained inside the Igman demilitarised zone illegally until June or July 1995? So from the 5th of October, 1994, until the summer of 1995, and only then under pressure did they withdraw.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1994, the Bosnian forces withdrew from Krupa after a military operation conducted by the United Nations. As far as the entire demilitarised area is concerned, the directives that had been given were the following: We had to detect any form of infiltration in the demilitarised zone, whatever side this came from, and this is indeed what we did. Every time we noticed an illegal location, we tried to make sure that the Serb staff or Bosnian staff leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the Defence claims that that was not the case, that very difficult negotiations were conducted, that they refused to withdraw for several months and that that was the reason for our falling out with them, and that is to say, the deterioration of the relations.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were tough negotiations, as you say, but the UN mandate and the mandate of the UN soldiers was to protect the neutrality of the DMZ. And during the negotiations, we were still trying to detect those people who had infiltrated the area to make sure that they leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you familiar with this drawing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I actually saw it. I might have even been the person who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this link between AMZ [as interpreted] and ABiH zone was under the UN control and that that was both the exit and entry point in and out of Sarajevo that was used by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina military extensively?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. This area, i.e., the DMZ and the airport area, were placed under the authority of the United Nations. Notwithstanding the negotiations that may have taken place regarding the crossing, we tried to make sure that these areas, and more specifically the DMZ, remain free from any movement or passage on the part of the Bosnians or the Serbs, and that was essentially the mandate of the UN at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this drawing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3396.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Witness, sir, I'm going to state the position of the Defence. The Defence asserts that Sarajevo was not under siege, that was there a regular manoeuvre by the forces of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army with whole units entering and exiting with their weaponry through this link between Dobrinja and Butmir. And now can we look at the English version as well. Just one illustration. On the 21st of March, the commander of the 102nd Brigade orders 400 soldiers and officers to leave the city of Sarajevo and to go to the zone of the 16th Division, up north, thus to take out a section, with the 60-millimetre weaponry and 102-millimetre weapons with them, and they were even going to carry out a review in the yard of the Pavle Goranin school, and then when the review is over, they're going to do a joint march and then take the Sarajevo-Butmir-Krupac-Kiseljak --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly note we don't see the text that Mr. Karadzic is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this column had to pass the Igman road?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to confirm that the column passed through the Igman road. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there any other road from Hrasnica or from Butmir leading out other than the Igman road? You can see Sarajevo, Butmir, Krupac, Kiseljak, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly another alternative to the Igman road, one that was not controlled by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene. If I could seek a redaction at page 55, lines 10 through 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the road, any road, any road that is being used for this type of manoeuvre, can it be considered a military target from the military point of view?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question as to how to define targets, how parties define targets, sorry. I mean, our responsibility as the UN was for the Igman road, only for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Again, it seems to me that there's -- that the witness couldn't confirm the movement, the specific movement which was put to him, nor could he confirm the issue of the legitimacy of targeting. So there's no basis at the moment for admitting it, but it may well be that you can adduce it through another method.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you commented on numerous documents that you had not previously seen, that were presented to you by the OTP. May I call up now 1D3400 so that we can see if you can comment on this too. This is a document of the 12th Division a month after that first one, thus they are relieving men on a monthly basis, and this is a change-of-shift plan according to the brigades, and you can see the 28th of April of the 115th Brigade; the battalion on the 26th of April; the 105th Brigade from Sarajevo on the 30th of April; 102nd Brigade from Sarajevo on May 2nd, 1995. Could all of these soldiers pass by any other road other than the link between Hrasnica and Igman? Was there any other route for these soldiers to take out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN knew that the road they controlled was fully observed. Should there have been any troop movements, there would have been reports by the units on the ground. In other words, it could be that if there were rotations, they were done following other roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the English version and look at the last two lines and then move to the following page. "The battalion from Sarajevo shall leave at 1900 hours on buses of the -- although it is buses, DB, Dobrinja-Butmir feature, strictly moving along the road to Butmir. From there they shall march on foot to Radeljevaca, and so on and so forth. If this Radeljevaca is on the Igman road, would you then accept that they had to take the Igman road?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that if they had taken that road, the UN units being on the ground would have reported such movements, and I do not have any recollection to the effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to be fair to you, Witness, I accept the possibility that you were not always properly informed, so we're going to show the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document being admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It falls into exactly the same category as the last document, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we now have 65 ter 000 -- 65 ter 11070, and can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, I'm going to show you one of the sources of possible misunderstanding and lack of information, information that was denied to you. Can you please look at this document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are the Muslim forces, the 1st Corps, of the 30th of September, 1994. These are instructions or a supplement to the order, supplement to the order relating to conduct towards the UNPROFOR forces. Guide units which are inserted into the temporarily occupied territory - it is actually Serbian territory but this is how they referred to it - through the 20-kilometre exclusion zone running parallel to the UNPROFOR forces in complete secrecy. Conceal and disguise the bringing in and deployment of units. Units which are attacking from the front in the zone of exclusion and in the UNPA zones, according to the agreement of the 13th of August, 1993, shall also take measures of concealment while they are brought in, advancing and approaching until the units are led to the initial positions and, rather, JP. And then it says if UNPROFOR forces try physically by using force to prevent you from carrying out a task you shall respond in kind to all of their actions. "Respond to diversionary operations by UNPROFOR with diversionary operations. "Return fire when fire is opened on our forces troops and hardware in order to protect the lives of our soldiers and carry out tasks." Witness, do you agree that the Muslim side took quite systematic measures to conceal from you their illegal activities in the total exclusion zone and in the DMZ in Igman?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
