utterances.text: I can't express an opinion as to what the Bosnian units wanted to do or may have done. Remember that the UN mandate was to do everything they could to prevent any movement in the demilitarised zone. And as to our troops, we did not have many. It was impossible to cover and observe the entirety of the zone. Therefore, if Bosnian forces managed to go through the DMZ to go somewhere else, well, we had some suspicions about it, but we did everything we could in order to be able to detect such unit. It may be that they transited outside the places where we would observe what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: It's not just the DMZ, but it's also the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. Thus, in the centre of town all these movements and manoeuvres were concealed from you in all possible ways. Does this document confirm that Muslim forces concealed from the United Nations their heavy weaponry and the movements and their attacks in the forbidden areas, in the DMZs, and in the total exclusion zones? All I'm asking you is does this document confirm that you were prevented from being informed about their illegal activities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the logical problem with the formulation of that question I think is fairly obvious and I saw from the Court's reaction that you were about to intervene for the same reason so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, to ask a witness to confirm he didn't know something is getting to be a logical impossibility. If you don't know something -- if you have no knowledge of something, it stands alone. You cannot confirm that you didn't know something. You cannot deny that you didn't know something if you had no information on which to base a state of knowledge. So it seems to be a fruitless line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, in line 8 on this page 59, you said that you are unable to voice your opinion about what the Bosnian units intended. Does that mean that you cannot voice your opinion about what the Serb units wanted either?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a witness, I am not able to know what other people's intentions were. I know one thing; namely, that what the UN units saw they reported on. Now, as to suppose or speculate as to things that I have not seen or witnessed, I cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you received this document in early October 1994 would you have known considerably more? Would your position have been different?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not receive it, how do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at your amalgamated statement, page 22, paragraph 2 from the bottom where you confirm --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we need to go into -- for several seconds, for a minute, for several minutes into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If there's a risk that we need to, we need to. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document, 11070, that talks about the attitude towards UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Momentarily lost track of that document. I can't see that it falls outside the -- it seems to fall within the same category as the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's certainly my view, Dr. Karadzic. Again, this may well be a document which, as alluded to before by Mr. Tieger, would be better suited to, as other documents are, bar table motions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, I believe this witness said earlier, on the first day, that the Muslims were in a position to deceive them, but let it stay as you wish. Can we look at 1D1044 before the break, please. There is also a translation. This is a document of the command of the 1st Corps. There is an English version too. We must put the English version on the ELMO, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 15th of June, 1995. The command of the 1st Corps confirms that they are still at Igman and that they even have a forward command post there, Igman. This is the fourth line from the top: "[In English] Forward command post Igman." [Interpretation] Is it correct that in mid-June they were still in the DMZ, the Igman DMZ, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report from the Bosnian forces. As far as I know, there is no correspondent report from the UN, but I can't express an opinion on this document which is not a UN document, and -- that I'm not aware of. I didn't know of it before, and I didn't know of it until today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Witness, sir, you did comment on Serb documents that you were seeing for the first time. What I'm asking you now is this: Did you have knowledge that this document was correct? Did you know that in mid-June they were still at Igman, the Muslim forces were still at Igman?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question. If he says so, it may be right, but I'm not sure. I don't know. I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave the document for a moment. Were they there at the time, or did you drive them away from Igman earlier or later? I'm not talking about Krupac. I'm talking about the DMZ at Igman, where they have a forward command post.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for advice as to what should the Defence do if we believe that a witness is biased and that, for example, he authenticates the Serbian documents and he doesn't do the same with the Muslim documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's not a helpful comment which Mr. Tieger is no doubt about to emphasise. The short answer is that if you suspect somebody of being biased, you put a direct question to them and receive a direct answer. We're now going to rise for half an hour. We've considered the position as to whether or not to allow any further time for cross-examination, and we are prepared to grant a further 30 minutes, which will start from the moment we re-enter the court. The court will sit until 3.00. It will be necessary to have a short adjournment between 2.00 and 2.10 for a tape change, and we will reassemble at five minutes past the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you still stand by your position that due to the meandering line of confrontation, it was difficult to determine where fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do confirm what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to put his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Judge's microphone please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think the witness's microphone is not -- I don't know whose control is -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat -- [Interpretation] Can you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm that the confrontation line was a sinusoidal line, and it was difficult to determine the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Mr. Witness, did you know what the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps strength was? Were you familiar with its strength, its composition, and its deployment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did indeed have information which was provided to us by the liaison officers of UNPROFOR who were with the various parties. Whether this was or certainty and entire truth, I don't know. I had a vague understanding of the locations as provided by our liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what the strength and area of deployment was of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be afraid of making a mistake. I don't remember. We, the UN forces, were peace partners for both sides. We did not conduct an analysis as an opponent would do in the standard fashion. This was not our objective at all and not the objective of our assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the first row of hills around the town of Sarajevo was under the Muslim control, that is to say, the BH Army? If it would be easier for you, I can give you the names: Igman, Mojmilo, Hrasno Brdo, Debelo Brdo, Colina Kapa, Mala Kapa. That's to the south; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be as positive about all those names after all the years that have elapsed, but what was on Bosnian territory was held by the population. Inside that area there might have been Bosnian units, but I cannot ascertain that with a hundred per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Debelo Brdo is a dominant feature over the central part, including Skenderija, and that on the northern slopes of Debelo Brdo were Muslims and that the Serbs were on the southern slope?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important thing for the UN forces was the position of the UN forces which was located on the summit of Debelo Brdo. Therefore, at a distance which I cannot calculate now, very close distance, there were Bosnians in the northern area and Serb forces in the southern area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on the northern side there were a number of dominant elevations held by the BH Army, and I can also enumerate them starting from east to west, off the top of my head; Sedam Suma, Grdonj Hill, Sedrenik, Hum, Brijesce Brdo, Zuc, Orlic, Sokolje. This whole range on the north. Do you agree that all these dominant features were under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were in the north. They were controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but if it is a matter of identifying those locations with precision, I must say that my memory doesn't serve me that well now. That would be difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that in Sarajevo there was the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there was the Main Staff of the 1st Corps, the staff of the 12th Division, and the staff of all the accompanying installations and staff units of the 101st, 102nd, 105th, 115th, 152nd, 111th, and 112th Brigades? Are you familiar with the names of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone knew the name of his brigades. Depending on the level of responsibility, we knew where such and such a unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that with regard to an inquiry from the United Nations, you were informed by the Muslim army that the buildings around the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the close proximity of Holiday Inn, were under the control of the police rather than the army, and that any sniper shooters that might be operating there would be from the police, not from the military? That was a response to a protest issued by the United Nations to the effect that sniper nests were located there, and the BH Army informed the United Nations that those belonged to the police and not to the army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember this information. This was a subject of concern for all the people working for the United Nations. We tried to detect the positions or the sniper nests on either side. This was a concern for all the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the Serbian side offered truce in Sarajevo on several occasions and that they even proclaimed cease-fire in and around Sarajevo unilaterally?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect this exactly, what the document stated and what documents were provided and what information these documents contained. I know that during a fairly long period of time outside peaks of activity, there was a decrease in the pressure exerted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say, and now we are talking about the relevant period, that the Muslim side never offered truce in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. Perhaps it did. Perhaps it didn't. As far as the level of responsibility is concerned, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the previously reached agreements between the parties and the United Nations? Specifically, did you know that there was a protocol accompanying the agreement on the total exclusion zone from March 1994, February 1994?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were informed that from the Jewish Cemetery, the Serbs targeted the building of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency by using the so-called Maljutka, which is a wire-guided missile?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. I can confirm that. I do confirm that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the building of the Presidency there was also the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that on both those grounds the Presidency building was a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that I did acknowledge that a round was fired. Now, whether to draw a conclusion on the identity of the inhabitants, that is something else. I know that there were members of the government and the Presidency there. Where the various offices and personalities were housed, I cannot actually say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this information could have been misinformation, having in mind numerous buildings, pylons, and installations of all kinds, and that a wire-guided missile from the Jewish Cemetery all the way to the Presidency building didn't have much chance of hitting the target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was reported to the UN forces and their representatives was that the shot originated from an area which was occupied by the Serb forces. Despite firing difficulties, we acknowledged that this shot had been fired. This was an observation on the part of UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the fact that in the city of Sarajevo, inside the total inclusion zone -- exclusion zone, there were numerous plants and workshops that manufactured weapons and various types of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a rumour circulated in the town of Sarajevo. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) This rumour did circulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall and were you informed that there were two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. A redaction, please, at page 73, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think you -- I'm not sure you have the right line there, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's actually different on two different screens, but I think you're looking at line -- line 3; correct. That's how it shows on the LiveNote, but on the version that's broadcast on the opposite screen in court it came out as line 1, but according to the LiveNote we've been going on, it is line -- it would be line 3; correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness, that there were numerous independent battalions in Sarajevo and that there were also two Special Police brigades that had been equipped by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that used them in combat? One of those units was called Lasta, and the other one was called Bosna.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN forces all saw policemen in Sarajevo, Muslim policemen in fairly large numbers. We did not know the names of these units, and we didn't know what their purpose was. This information was never disclosed to us, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3403 for a moment, and after that 3407. There should be a translation as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it right that what we see here is the command of the 12th Division issuing an order to prepare firing positions for 105 howitzer gun in co-ordination -- or, rather, with the last order immediately camouflage the artillery piece in -- and protect it against reconnaissance by UN forces. And listed below are axes where they're going to open fire, which are, in fact, the Serbian villages that were to be the targets. Do you agree that it was impermissible for them to do that in the exclusion zone, and the fact that they wanted to hide this from the United Nations constituted an illegal action?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two parts to my question. The first thing is that I see this document for the first time. The second thing is that if it is true to fact, the Bosnian forces were violating the initial protocol relating to the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise to make the same point, but it's -- it's another in a line of similar submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, what the witness has said is that if it's true, then the Bosnian forces were violating the initial protocol, which may be self-evident. But it doesn't assist in the admission of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like also to show 3407, just so that we can see for ourselves that the 2nd Police Brigade, the Bosna Brigade, was under the command of the army and that the army equipped it with banned weapons in the total exclusion zone. Let's just wait for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have Bosna here, and it's supposed to form a company using the following units: 120-millimetre mortar, 82-millimetre mortar, four pieces, and this is being relocated to the Bosna brigade, which is a police brigade. Does this also present a violation of the total exclusion zone agreement, and before that, can you look at what brigade is supposed to be given what. The 105th is supposed to provide the commander and an 82-millimetre mortar, then also the 105th is giving a squad commander and 120-millimetre mortar, and so on and so forth. Does this also not represent the flagrant violation of the total exclusion zone agreement and concealment of all of this from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat the answer I gave earlier. I'm seeing this document for the first time, and if it is true, this is a violation of the protocol relating to the exclusion zone. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the same must apply as far as admissibility is concerned, Dr. Karadzic. Now, looking at the time, make this your last question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Although I believe that that is a pity, but, all right. We will now manage somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, do you remember that President Carter managed to broker a truce in late December 1994 and that we all enjoyed the benefits of that truce for quite some time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the arrival of President Carter very well. I think it was on the 19th of December, 1994, and there was a combination of what the president had achieved and the weather conditions which led to a substantial lull during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 1D3394. If I were to say to you, Witness, sir, that the Muslim side did not take part in the truce sincerely and that this document would show that, would you agree that we also had the right to be angry and to be cautious and to be distrustful, because if one cannot obey the agreement brokered by President Carter, what could we hope for? Would you agree that this truce was betrayed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the facts observe by UN personnel on the ground demonstrated that both sides or neither side had complied with the entire agreement. What the share of responsibility of one or other side is I cannot calculate this, and I cannot assess in mathematical terms the level of responsibility of one or other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you, please, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, there must be some error in translation of the English "last question" into Serbian. This is definitively your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I was thinking about the last document. That's why I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Witness, sir, that this document attests to the fact that on the 6th of January, an order was issued on full readiness, full combat readiness, and that nobody is in possession of a similar document by the Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, and for simply agreeing the document says what it purportedly says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second half of the question, perhaps, but the first part talks about preparations a week after the four-month truce was brokered.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I repeat what my position is: If this document is true to fact, it is difficult to say whether there is any breach of the protocol. I'm a witness. How can I assess a document of a general nature which I see for the first time today? You are asking me to assess this document. I think this is rather utopian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, does the same general principle apply, that if this document were, in fact, a true and accurate account, then it would suggest a breach of protocol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I said before I provided my answer. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you admit -- can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it by definition falls into exactly same category of the other documents dealt with in the same way by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have just a very few follow-up questions. During the course of your cross-examination, you were shown D1117. And if that could be called up on the screen, please. It's a document dated the 26th of April, 1995, sent by General Nikolai to General Delic. And if we can scroll down to the bottom. CC'd to Lieutenant-General Milovanovic. And the subject was "Heavy weapon violations of safe areas/exclusion zones." And if we could next, and just to -- so you can compare it to the next document, you can see the first paragraph is over -- begins with "Over the last two months," then "Protest letters," then "I want to emphasise," then "Therefore," and so on. If we could next call up -- and, Witness, that document was presented to you in the context of explaining -- about the accused explaining or at least suggesting what Muslims were doing, what Bosnian forces were doing and what Bosnian Serb forces were not. So I'd like to show you 65 ter 90239. And, Witness, there we see another document dated 26 April 1995, also sent by General Nikolai. Subject again is "Heavy weapon violations of safe areas/exclusion zones." The text appears to be identical, but this one is sent to Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic in Pale. And if we scroll down we see that it was cc'd to General Delic. Witness, do these appear to be similar or precisely the same protests sent to both sides on the same date, and are the two documents, when seen together, a further reflection of UN impartiality that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that all the UN high representatives wanted to remain impartial. Whenever an event would occur, this gave an opportunity to remind both parties of the rules they had to comply with. Therefore, whatever their level, all people in charge would follow the same policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document, 90239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, the, as it were, sister document was admitted, was it not? Yes. That will be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you were also asked quite a number of questions about convoys and restrictions of humanitarian aid and questions about Bosnian Muslim responsibility for restrictions and Bosnian Serb interest in supposed or alleged interest in maintaining full humanitarian aid access. Let me show you a couple of documents if I may. The first is 65 ter 19424. Witness, this is a code cable dated the 6th of July, 1995, from Mr. Akashi in Zagreb to Mr. Annan in New York, and it describes the situation in Bihac, and then on the second page in the eastern enclaves and then going on to Sarajevo. Turn to the second page, please. And it begins in describing the situation in Sarajevo by saying: "The suspension of the UNHCR air-lift to Sarajevo since 8 April has affected UNHCR's capacity to deliver food supplies to the city." And if we can -- then it describes some of the problems. If we continue to the next page. To the middle of the page. The document also describes an agreement reached with the Bosnian Serbs on the 8th of June for convey access, and then continues in approximately the middle of that first paragraph: "However, despite this agreement, the Bosnian Serb authorities still continued to obstruct access and demanded 50 per cent of deliveries rather than the usual 23 per cent based on a needs assessment. When clearances were finally obtained, convoys were blocked because of the BiH offensive around Sarajevo." And the document continues, if we look at the first sentence of the next paragraph: "UNHCR has not received clearance from the Bosnian Serb side to deliver aid to Sarajevo since 20 June, and the humanitarian situation in the city has become very serious." And that paragraph ends: "UNHCR is today facing the most serious disruption in its food distribution in Sarajevo since its assistance programme began in 1992. Another aspect of the situation which is of great concern to UNHCR is the current level of shelling which the civilian population has been subjected to in recent days." Witness, does that -- is that consistent with your recollection of events with respect to Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: KDZ182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concords perfectly with the situation. I would not want anyone to believe that freedom of movement, which was indeed somewhat limited by the Bosnians, within Sarajevo would have been far less than the freedom of movement called by the Bosnian Serbs outside Sarajevo. So whether -- whether it was about restricting road access or air-lift to provide supplies. There was no proportionality with regard to freedom of movement. The freedom of movement caused by the Serbs was far greater than the freedom of movement limited by the Bosnians within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 19424, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has confirmed the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Witness. That concludes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings your testimony to an end. Thank you for coming to The Hague. It is not easy when you have to move between private and open session all the time, but I want to thank your colleagues also for their help. And I wish you all a very good day. [In English] There are technical arrangements which need to be put in place for the next witness. I'm advised that ten minutes will do it. So we'll rise now and sit again at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Hello, Madam Witness. If you would like, please, to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to sit and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I've got a few questions for you about the evidence you've previously given to this Tribunal. Do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in June of 1997, and following that, do you recall testifying before this Tribunal in the Krajisnik case in April 2005?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that this year, 2011, on February 4th and 5th, you had read back to you a further statement by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor consolidating this earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you added a small amount of additional information at that point?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes, because that pertained to the period up until the very end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you signed that statement.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I was to ask you the same questions today as those which gave rise to the written evidence in that statement you listened to in February of this year, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Of course. Absolutely the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, that statement is 65 ter 90222. Could that be please be a Prosecution exhibit under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2444, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of that written evidence. This witness lived with her family in the area of Grbavica prior to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and remained there with her mother throughout the conflict and the period of reintegration in 1996. The witness describes her neighbourhood, its population and composition, and how non-Serbs -- non-Serbs were affected with the outbreak of war in 1992 and the takeover of Grbavica by Bosnian Serb forces. She provides details on the Bosnian Serb military presence in the area and the firm control exercised by the military. The witness not only saw but was subject to persecutions by Bosnian Serb forces, in particular from the late spring and into the autumn of 1992. These persecutory measures included arbitrary arrests as well as repeated house searches. She gives evidence of the expulsions of Muslims from Grbavica, including an incident on 30 September 1992, where Muslims were expelled by armed soldiers. On 11 June 1992, the witness and her mother were taken from their home at gunpoint by Veselin Vlahovic, otherwise known as Batko. Batko then raped, beat, threatened, and robbed both women, the witness and her mother. Batko, the witness concluded, was a member of the military. Following the incident, she saw Batko interviewed on TV. After the incident the witness tried repeatedly to leave Grbavica for Bosnian-held territory. The night of 30 September 1992, after seeing numbers of Muslims being driven out of the area, the witness and her mother were evicted from their flat by a man in military police uniform. The next morning, with nowhere to go, the witness visited the military police headquarters and asked to be expelled. She was told that this wasn't being done any longer and Grbavica was completely blocked. The witness describes her experiences of life for civilians in Bosnian-Serb-held Grbavica during the years of the conflict. She saw mortars in her neighbourhood and notes that there were tanks in the area all the time, from as early as May 1992. She talks of mortar and tank fire coming from Grbavica, of seeing snipers passing by. Everybody in Grbavica knew who the snipers were. They would walk in the streets with their special rifles. She saw them going up into the apartment building at Lenjinova 58, one of the locations from which the snipers operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, having read that summary, I'd like, Madam Witness, to ask you some questions relating to the matters that you discussed in the statement, in the written evidence that we filed. First, Madam Witness, did you ever report the incident involving Batko to Bosnian Serb -- local Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: On one occasion I went to the premises of the military police, which was on Zagrebacka Street, which was called the street of General Dragoljub Draza Mihajlovic during the war. I wanted to ask them what should my mother and I do. Since we didn't have any papers, we were not able to move around, and I had to go out occasionally to do some shopping for bread or -- and things like that. I asked them how could I obtain some ID. At first they listened to me, but then they asked me about my identification card, and I said I didn't have one. They kept asking for it, insisting on it. I said that we didn't have any IDs, that they had been confiscated from us, and I was speaking on behalf of my mother as well. They asked me who took them away, and then I started telling them the whole story. I burst into tears. Then they asked me if I had any problems. I tried to believe that they wanted to know what kind of problems I wanted, because everybody had problems had problems during the war. So in response to that inquiry, I mentioned the name of this -- I don't know how to call him, a human being or whatever, Veselin Vlahovic, and I said that he had taken my mother and me, but I couldn't put it into words immediately. While I was talking, they looked at me in a sort of way, and it occurred to me that people were looking at me in disbelief, wondering whether it is possible that somebody could have survived something that was done by such a criminal. That's what I felt. Now, this whole story started to unravel. I told them a number of things. One of those military policemen, his name was Boro Sljuka, and they all had ID cards or passes, badges on their jackets. He was making notes while I was talking. When I mentioned the name of the criminal, he put this paper that he had been writing on in a drawer in front of me. He then glanced at another policeman and said, "We're not going to take any more notes about this." And that's what happened on the occasion when I went to the military police and outlined what had happened to me to them. I just gave them the crux of the matter. I told them that my mother and I were the victims of a savage assault, a beastly assault by a man who used on top of everything abusive language and called us all kinds of names. So this is how I reported it then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: It could have been in July of 1992. In July 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, were you ever at any time approached by Bosnian Serb authorities with respect to any investigation into the incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. I realised and I said then that actually the wisest thing, if one can speak about that at all, not to mention this ever, and it was something that would be a fairytale, looking at it in hindsight, if I had expected anyone to do anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on in your statement, at paragraph 65 you referred to Batko and you said: "Based on the clothes and the weapons he carried, one could conclude that he was definitely a member of some organised military." When you used those orders "organised military," were you referring to anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: As someone who has no military experience, naturally, but by looking at a man in full uniform and with the insignia worn by others and carrying a rifle, what else could I have concluded other than what I did? It was only natural and normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You have just referred to insignia, that he was in uniform and bore the insignia worn by others. I wonder if you can recall what insignia those were.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Since he did not come only once, he came to our flat twice before he took us away, the first time round he had a rather long overcoat. He is a rather short person, and this coat did not suit him or did not fit him at all, and underneath he had an olive-drab uniform. Of course he had a rifle. The second time he came, he was dressed in a camouflage uniform with the insignia on his sleeve reading "The Army of Republika Srpska," and there was a flag as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Further in your statement, at paragraph 92, you referred to a lot of mortar and tank fire from Grbavica onto the other side, and I was wondering whether you saw where those weapons you referred to were located.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say something about the tanks that were passing along this road nonstop. And this road that used to be the street along which trolley buses ran was the road that everyone had to cross in order to reach the central point in Grbavica where the open-air market was, and on the premises of the former local commune there was a church. Therefore, everybody had to travel down that road, speaking about pedestrians. Now, speaking about weaponry and tanks that later had some Cyrillic inscriptions like Black Djordje, Crni Djordje, whether that was after the tank driver or whoever, and weapons such as -- I even saw some weapons positioned between buildings, the passages between buildings that were leaning on pillars which created a certain space, and I suppose they would leave those weapons there if they were not in action. One could even see that those were equipped with very precise instruments. I saw it myself, and I think those were mortars that were on some kind of support, and close to a military staff that was headquartered in the offices of the former Digitron Buje company. That was the name of the company from Slovenia. What I want to say is that everyone who is familiar with Grbavica will know which location I'm referring to. So there's a staircase there that goes from this flat part of Grbavica to the Vraca neighbourhood. Now I've given you a more accurate location. One of those locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we just go back to something that you said that I actually don't quite understand. You said that you -- am I correct if I understand that you said you saw weapons positioned in passages between buildings that were leaning on pillars? Because I'm just wondering how passages could be leaning on pillars.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Yes. These are not standard passages. So at the end of a building it is protruding by some 3 or 4 metres, and it is leaning on pillars, and I referred to it as a passage in that sense. I didn't give you a proper technical term.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Further in your statement, at paragraphs 93 and 94, you mentioned seeing snipers passing by, walking in streets with special rifles and going up into the big apartment building at Lenjinova 58. How common were these special rifles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: That happened on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just stop you for a second. Perhaps I could rephrase. These -- what makes you describe these rifles as "special rifles"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: I couldn't find a better term, because these rifles were in kind of sheaths or holsters that served as the protection, but it was clear that there was a rifle inside, and all of us who would pass by could clearly see these soldiers bearing these rifles. Some people would recognise some of the soldiers from before, only now they were in uniforms. They knew their names and they knew some other details about these people and they knew what those people were involved in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were these special rifles carried by many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: No, no. After a while, we knew exactly, because overall that was such a long period of time and the area was small, so you start recognising things. As you recognised your neighbours before, you started recognising the faces of sharpshooters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Also at paragraph 93 you said that everybody in Grbavica knew who the snipers were. Do you, yourself, know who the snipers were by any chance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: One of those snipers was -- I don't know his full name. His first name was Marinko. He used to work for Dobrotvor. That's a Serbian charitable organisation that organised parcels to be sent in and out. Marinko used to work there at a later stage. There was also a man called Zlatko Subotic, and a friend of mine recognised him without doubt, and she used to live in Grbavica as well. And another rather painful thing was that there was a woman called Nada, who had worked before the war in a supermarket on Djura Djakovica Street. She was a sniper as well. The friend that I have just mentioned lived on Zagrebacka Street, number 30. From her balcony she saw that these snipers, the ones that I named, as well as a couple of others, or maybe seven or eight of them, would sometimes come to what would be a small shop in the basement. You have to go down the stairs. It's called Mak. And this is where they would hold some sort of meetings, and then they would all emerge from these premises together. This is something that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to go on to the final questions or area I have for you. It's in relation to paragraph 101 on your -- of your statement. You reported on an occasion where you saw Vojislav Seselj walking by your window, by your apartment window, accompanied by Slavko Aleksic. In that regard, perhaps you could tell us, to your knowledge, who was Slavko Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: That person was of striking appearance. Just before the war, I saw in the media, on television, I saw this man, and there was some mention of some titles like Vojvoda and things like that, which obviously meant a lot to him. Then I used to see that man in the marketplace. He would always be in the company of two other people. I suppose they were the -- his escort or his drivers. I don't know. He was driving in a Land Rover. There were not too many vehicles at the time, so I recognised it easily. But I also heard from another source about a man, because the brother of one of ours, that is to say, Dragan Markovic was a Serbian soldier. His wife was a Muslim. He told me that his brother Nedeljko or Nediljko Markovic was a personal escort of this Aleksic person since I saw him on the marketplace together with Aleksic, which means that I knew for sure who that person was and how he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just before we conclude, then, on this topic, I'd like to go to a video, 65 ter number 45107. It's in Sanction so we should all be able to follow the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We're going to go through this video, Madam Witness, and I'm going to stop the video at particular points and ask you at those particular points for -- a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. You can play.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've just paused at video at time-code 00:33.3. Madam Witness, we see on the video text on the top left-hand corner that says that it dates from 14 May 1993, and I wonder if you recognise the location that's depicted on the video screen at this point.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes, that is Zagrebacka Street. I think that on my left-hand side is the forestry faculty building, but you can't see it from the overgrown foliage on the streets. That's what they looked like at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So to your recollection, this film accurately depicts the situation on Zagrebacka Street in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what the street looked like. Although our movement was limited and everything would happen in the early morning hours or during early in the day, yes. I didn't see it at the time. I hear that the citizens welcomed him. I wasn't there when they welcomed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could continue the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something. I can see a building that I described a little bit earlier. This is how that part looked, the end of the building with the pillars. I'm talking about the building you can see. This is what those passages looked like, like extensions to the buildings in Grbavica, which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness has made that comment at time-code 00:54.4 of the video-clip. Perhaps we could continue then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you recognise any personalities that you see on the screen in front of you now at time-code 01:16.1?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Zagrebacka 30 building. I think that's what it is. The entrance is at the end of the building. Behind it is the building that I mentioned where the snipers had meetings. My friend saw that very clearly from her balcony. The persons that I recognise here are Slavko Aleksic on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If in --

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: This is the man in uniform with long black hair, with a cap.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on in the video, please, and it will go now for a couple of minutes before I ask the next question, and after that it's quite a short video.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at time-code 02:28.7, we've seen Mr. Seselj standing in front of a building giving an interview. Do you recognise the building where you see him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: That is the building number 2 in Grbavica -- or the building in Grbavica 2. This is what we called that part of Grbavica. It's a high-rise building behind a building we called Soping. I don't want to conceal the fact that my heart is beating very strongly. I wouldn't want to deny the words of Mr. Seselj who says himself, "Here are the military positions." I was just speaking about that myself in an attempt when I tried with a professor of mine, who actually was killed, Branko Krpan, I tried to cross over to the other side. When I tried do that, I passed through those. Today I ask myself how that was possible. We crossed. I'm thinking of those military positions. And then we entered the Soping area. This is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small intervention in the transcript with my apologies to the witness. The witness said died, not killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I know very well what I'm talking about. Professor Krpan, Mr. Karadzic, died after he left Grbavica, a year or so later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not your mistake. The translation was that he was killed, not that he died. It's not your mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can continue for precisely two more minutes on this video and we will be coming to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've stopped the film at time-code 04:10.5, and, Madam Witness, I'd like to ask you if you recognise the building depicted on the video at this time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entrance to the Soping. It's at that level when you climb the stairs. There were different shops there, furniture shops, post office, the bank. This is where I used to be in peacetime. That was that central area that people referred to as Soping.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this the same location you called Soping which you referred to in your statement when you described a military headquarters that you visited?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes. That is that place. It's just that we entered from the other side, which is to the right side of here. You also take the stairs up, and that also suited us because of the direction that we were coming from. In one of the furniture shops, actually in all of those furniture exhibition areas, which were quite large, instead of furniture there was some remnants of furniture. There were many soldiers who were sleeping there if there was a bed there that had been left in the show-room. There were some sleeping bags. Quite untidy-looking people with full combat equipment. I had the feeling there that they were lying there and waiting for something, waiting to go somewhere. That was the impression I got. And then at the end of the passage that we're talking about, when you climb the stairs and get to that level, there was a military headquarters, I guess, where we were sent by those who we had asked along the way how we could get to someone. They sent us to some commander who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to tender this 65 ter 45107 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2445.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, that's the examination-in-chief. There is but one associated exhibit of this witness, and I would seek to tender that associated exhibit. Would you like me to identify the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 21552. A map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Are we going to see that now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's an associated exhibit referred to in her statement. If you would like it displayed, Your Honour, I'm quite happy to do that and to have her comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just to make sure that this is -- it's been identified by the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it we could call up, then, 65 ter 21552, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you recognise the map that you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Grbavica area. Of course, this is showing a slightly wider area. I wasn't there. Grbavica. What it is, yes, it's Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: My sense of direction is clear about the position of the streets, the names of the streets, also the main features that are drawn in partially are drawn in and are not drawn in and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take from your answer, then, these are markings that you made?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is this the map, Madam Witness, that's referred to on a number of points during the course of your amalgamated statement that you signed in February of this year?

utterances.speaker: KDZ354
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that sufficient, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Then that can be admitted together with the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, you're going to have an opportunity to cross-examine on the map if you want to, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm just asking about the legend. Can we just know what the numbers mean. Have the map in the material, because if I don't have access ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, can you simply identify them quickly, Ms. Edgerton, what the numerals attached to the markings indicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'll have to go back to the witness's amalgamated statement and go through that paragraph by paragraph. I can't do it as quickly as Your Honours want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, in that case let's leave it for the moment because that's a task that can be undertaken and reduced into a short form. It's plain that we're not going to complete this witness's testimony today in any event. I'm sorry, Ms. Edgerton, did you say you'd concluded?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be Exhibit P2446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like -- plainly you're not going to come anywhere close to finishing today, but it's worthwhile using the 12 minutes or so that we have for you to start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would rather prefer, Excellency, if I start tomorrow and finish tomorrow in one piece, but if I have to, I will start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's not a question of whether you have to. I mean, if you feel that you are -- you would be able to do a more concise job by us rising now and then starting afresh tomorrow, then so be it. If that is the position, I was simply giving you an opportunity to warm-up today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just because I received the additional pages this morning. So I would prefer, then, to begin tomorrow, only for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Very well. Well, Madam Witness, impossible for us to have finished your testimony today, so inevitably you have to come back tomorrow morning. Have a peaceful evening, and we will meet again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.50 p.m.,
